card.title: Reported speech — backshifting without breaking meaning

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Reporting moves speech one step into the past: present→past, past→past perfect, will→would, can→could — because the reporting verb ('said') already sits in the past. Pronouns, places and times slide with the perspective (I→he, here→there, today→that day). Daily life reports constantly ('She said she was tired', 'They told me to wait'); mastering backshift is mastering everyday retelling.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: say + statement → said (that) + backshifted clause  ·  am/is→was · are→were · V1→V2 · V2→had+V3 · will→would · can→could · today→that day · tomorrow→the next day · here→there  ·  'I am tired' → He said (that) he was tired

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Backshift fires only under a PAST reporting verb; 'She says she IS tired' stays present. Universal truths and still-true facts resist shifting ('He said the earth moves round the sun'). Orders become infinitives ('told me to wait'), yes/no questions become if/whether clauses with statement word-order.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Questions lose their question order on reporting ('Where are you?' → 'asked where I was' — never 'where was I'). 'Said to me' becomes 'told me'; bare 'said' takes no object. Requests soften to 'asked/requested + infinitive'. Exclamations reframe as 'exclaimed with joy/sorrow that…'.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: 'I am tired,' he said → He said (that) he was tired: pronoun I→he, present am→past was, 'that' optional. Two moves, both mandatory — miss the pronoun and the reporter claims the tiredness; miss the tense and the timeline breaks. Test both directions: direct↔indirect.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Mechanical backshifting mangles still-true statements and habitual truths — meaning overrides the rule. Tone, sarcasm and emphasis evaporate in reported form ('Yeah, right' cannot backshift). Some languages report without shifting at all; English insists.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Derive the shift from timeline logic: the report happens AFTER the speech, so every time-reference steps back one notch along the tense ladder (present→past→past perfect), then stops — past perfect cannot shift further. Pronoun/place/time slides follow the same single principle: re-anchor every deictic word to the reporter's standpoint.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Ladder drill: will→would, can→could, V1→V2, V2→had+V3 — chant it. Questions: if/whether + statement order. Orders: told/asked + to-infinitive. Check pronouns LAST (most forgotten mark) — re-read with 'who is who?'.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: NEB-style: direct↔indirect pairs ('I am tired' → reported; 'Where are you going?' → asked-form); orders as infinitives; said-to→told conversion. Narration + tense backshift is the highest-frequency grammar pair.
